templates.title: Build a prospect list from LinkedIn into a sheet
templates.outcome: A deduped tracker sheet of every match with name, title, company, and profile URL
templates.prompt:
Go to my open LinkedIn search results tab.

Page through all results (keep clicking "show more" until exhausted). For every person matching [criteria, e.g. "VP or above, 200+ employee SaaS companies"], extract: full name, title, company, location, profile URL.

De-duplicate against anyone already in [existing sheet link, or leave blank for none], then write everything into a new Google Sheet titled "[search name] — Prospects" with one row per person and a Status column I can use for outreach tracking.

If a profile is out of network and shows no title, still capture the name and URL and mark the row Needs enrichment rather than dropping it.

templates.title: Enrich my company list with decision-maker contacts
templates.outcome: Your sheet filled with up to 3 verified decision-makers per company
templates.prompt:
Read my sheet at [sheet link]. It has one company per row.

For each company, find up to 3 people in [target roles, e.g. "Head of Ops, VP Finance, COO"]. Use LinkedIn as the source of truth for title and current employment — do not carry over a title from a stale directory listing.

Write each contact into new columns on that row: name, title, LinkedIn URL, and how confident you are that they still hold the role. Leave the row untouched and mark it Not found rather than guessing a plausible-sounding name.

Stop and tell me if more than a third of the list comes back empty — that usually means the role filter is wrong for this segment.

templates.title: Check my outreach replies and update my tracker
templates.outcome: Tracker rows updated with each reply, plus drafted follow-ups for the interested ones
templates.prompt:
Check my Gmail for replies to outbound threads from the last [7] days.

For each reply, find the matching row in [tracker sheet link] and update its Status to one of: Interested, Not now, Referred on, or Declined. Add the reply date and a one-line summary of what they actually said — not your interpretation of it.

For every Interested reply, draft a follow-up in Gmail that answers whatever they asked and proposes a concrete next step. Leave it as a draft; do not send.

If a reply does not match any tracker row, list it at the end so I can see who is contacting me outside the campaign.

templates.title: Send 15 personalized connection requests every morning
templates.outcome: A steady drip of tailored LinkedIn invites, capped daily and logged to your tracker
templates.prompt:
Open [prospect sheet link] and take the next 15 rows with an empty Invite Sent column.

For each person, open their LinkedIn profile and read their recent activity. Send a connection request with a note that references something specific and real from their profile or a recent post — not their job title, and not a compliment that would fit anyone.

Log the date and the exact note text back to the row.

Stop at 15 for the day even if there are more rows. If someone is already a connection, or has a pending invite, skip them and mark the row rather than sending again.

templates.title: Draft replies to every sales thread waiting on me
templates.outcome: Gmail drafts ready for review on each thread where a prospect is waiting on you
templates.prompt:
Find every Gmail thread where a prospect wrote last and I have not replied, going back [14] days.

For each one, read the whole thread before drafting — including anything I said earlier that I now need to honour. Write a reply that answers their actual question, moves to a specific next step with a date, and matches the tone of how I have been writing in that thread.

Save each as a Gmail draft on the existing thread. Send nothing.

Where a thread needs information I do not have — pricing I have not quoted, a date I have not confirmed — leave a clearly marked blank in the draft rather than inventing it, and list those threads for me at the end.

templates.title: Nudge prospects who went silent after my last email
templates.outcome: Polite bump drafts queued for every outbound thread with no reply in 4+ days
templates.prompt:
Find outbound Gmail threads where I sent the last message [4] or more days ago and got no reply.

Skip anyone who has replied at any point in the thread, anyone who asked me to follow up later than today, and anyone I have already bumped twice — a third nudge is not persistence.

For the rest, draft a short bump on the existing thread. Add one new thing: a relevant piece of news about their company, a resource, or a narrower ask. Never send "just bumping this to the top of your inbox" with nothing else in it.

Leave everything as drafts and give me the list.

templates.title: Turn my conference notes into follow-up email drafts
templates.outcome: A personalized Gmail draft for every contact in your event notes, logged row by row
templates.prompt:
Read my notes at [notes doc link] from [event name].

Pull out every person I met: name, company, and what we actually talked about. Where I only wrote a first name and a company, find the full name and email — check the event site, the company site, then LinkedIn, in that order.

Draft a Gmail follow-up to each one that references the specific thing we discussed, not the event in general. Keep it under 120 words.

Log everyone to a sheet with name, company, email, the talking point, and whether a draft was created. Anyone I could not find contact details for goes on the sheet too, marked Needs email — those are the ones worth chasing by hand.

templates.title: Scrub my target list against CRM and past outreach
templates.outcome: A cleaned list with existing customers, open deals, and recent touches flagged out
templates.prompt:
Take the company list at [sheet link].

For each row, check HubSpot for an existing company record and flag: already a customer, open deal in progress, closed-lost in the last [6] months, or no record. Then check my Gmail for any thread with that domain in the last [90] days and note the date and who it was with.

Write the findings into new columns and add a Contact column with a clear yes or no, plus the reason.

Do not delete rows — I want to see what was excluded and why. A list that silently shrinks is one I cannot audit.

templates.title: Refresh my outreach tracker while I sleep
templates.outcome: Every row re-checked overnight with a next action, stale flags, and backup contacts
templates.prompt:
Go through every row in [tracker sheet link] that is not marked Closed.

For each: re-check the prospect's LinkedIn for a job change, look for a reply in Gmail I have not logged, and work out the right next action from where the conversation actually stands. Write that next action into the row in plain language, with a date.

Flag any row with no activity in [21] days as Stale. If someone has changed company, mark the row Left — and find the person now holding that role, as a new row.

Do not change the Status column; that is mine to set. Everything you write goes in the columns you own.

templates.title: Watch my target accounts for buying signals on LinkedIn
templates.outcome: A morning brief of intent posts from your watch list with a suggested angle for each
templates.prompt:
Read the account list at [sheet link].

For each company, check LinkedIn for posts in the last [7] days from the company page and from anyone on the list holding [target roles]. Look for signals that mean something: hiring for a role that implies a new initiative, a funding or launch announcement, a leadership change, or someone publicly describing a problem we solve.

Ignore reposts, anniversaries and generic thought leadership. A brief padded with noise stops being read.

Give me a morning summary grouped by company: the signal, the link, and one specific angle to open with. If nothing real happened, say so — an empty brief is a useful answer.

templates.title: Apply to partner programs from my list and log status
templates.outcome: Applications submitted across your list with per-row status and blockers logged
templates.prompt:
Work through the partner programs listed at [sheet link], oldest row first.

For each one, open the application page and complete it using the details in [company info doc link]. Where a field asks something not covered by that doc — an integration timeline, a customer count — stop on that row, mark it Needs input, and note exactly what is missing. Do not invent business facts.

Submit only when every field is filled from real information, then log the submission date, a confirmation number if there is one, and any next steps they state.

Work through at most [5] applications in one run.

templates.title: Turn inbound lead alerts into CRM deals
templates.outcome: Every demo request and form fill from your inbox filed as a deal in the right stage
templates.prompt:
Search my Gmail for demo requests, form fills and contact-us notifications from the last [7] days.

For each one, pull out the person's name, email, company and whatever they said they wanted. Check HubSpot for an existing contact or company — if one exists, note it rather than creating a duplicate.

Tell me which stage each should sit in and why, based on what they asked for: a pricing question is not the same as a trial signup.

Give me the list to confirm before anything is written to HubSpot. Filing a lead in the wrong stage quietly skews every forecast that reads off it.

templates.title: Build a niche company list with the right buyer at each
templates.outcome: A researched sheet of niche-market companies, each with the likely decision-maker
templates.prompt:
Build me a list of companies matching [description, e.g. "US independent pharmacies with 3-20 locations"].

Find at least [40]. Work from real sources — industry directories, association member lists, trade bodies — and record where each one came from. Do not pad the list to hit the number.

For each company: name, website, location, rough size, and the person most likely to own [the relevant decision], with their title and LinkedIn URL.

Put it in a sheet with a Source column. Where you could not identify a decision-maker, leave it blank and say so — a blank is honest and a wrong name costs me the first email.

templates.title: Score every lead in my sheet with a tier and an angle
templates.outcome: Your list graded A to C with one researched fact and an outreach angle per company
templates.prompt:
Read the leads at [sheet link].

Grade each A, B or C against [criteria, e.g. "50+ employees, uses Shopify, has a marketing team"]. Say in one line why it got that grade, referencing what you actually found rather than restating the criteria.

For every A and B, add one specific researched fact about the company from the last [6] months — a launch, a hire, an expansion, a public complaint — and one outreach angle that follows from it.

Write the grade, the reason, the fact and the angle into new columns. Leave C rows without an angle; spending research on them is the thing that stops the As getting done.

templates.title: Find warm paths into my target accounts
templates.outcome: A map of who you already know at each target company, with intro asks drafted
templates.prompt:
Take the target companies at [sheet link].

For each, check my LinkedIn connections for anyone who works there now, worked there in the last [2] years, or is a first-degree connection of someone who does. Note the relationship and how strong it looks — a former colleague is not the same as someone I connected with at a conference.

Where there is a credible path, draft a short Gmail intro request to the connection: who I want to reach, why, and an easy way for them to say no.

List the companies with no warm path separately. Those are the cold ones and it is better to know that up front.

templates.title: Work my local business outreach queue every Monday
templates.outcome: The next 15 queue rows enriched with owner contacts and draft emails, status logged
templates.prompt:
Open [queue sheet link] and take the next [15] rows with an empty Contacted date.

For each business: find the owner or manager's name and a direct email — check the company website first, then any professional listing. A generic info@ is a last resort, and mark it as such.

Draft a Gmail email that names something specific about that business — what they sell, a recent review, how long they have been running. A template with the name swapped in reads exactly like what it is.

Write the contact details and the draft status back to the row. Anything with no findable contact gets marked Needs a call.
